--- title: "Responsible Use of AI for Non-Coders: AI in Your Workflow" subtitle: "
Bioinformatics Resource Center - Rockefeller University" author: - "[http://rockefelleruniversity.github.io/responsible_use_of_AI_for_noncoders/](http://rockefelleruniversity.github.io/responsible_use_of_AI_for_noncoders/)" - "[brc@rockefeller.edu](mailto:brc@rockefeller.edu)" --- ::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"} # Responsible Use of AI for Non-Coders: AI in Your Workflow ::: ## Overview *Presenter: Matt — 50 mins* - [What is a good workflow](#what-is-a-good-workflow) - [Hard lines](#hard-lines) - [Controlling what is allowed](#controlling-what-is-allowed) # Good workflows {background-color="#23373B" .center .middle} ## What is a good AI workflow A good AI workflow for bioinformatics largely replicates a good bioinformatics workflow. As with how we code more traditionally, taking short-cuts comes back to haunt us later. Very little of Bioinformatics is just 'plug and play'. Key cornerstones. - Planning - Reproducibility - Checkpoints and modularization - Understanding what your code is doing ## Planning As with all science approaches we need do make decisions about how we will address our problem. For example: "I have some scRNAseq data from mouse fat cells. I want to do some generate clusters of fat cell sub types" At this point you can decide what software to use (Seurat/Scanpy), what reference to use (mm10/mm39). Understanding the path of our analysis is important from the outset. If you are unfamiliar with the analysis the broad-stroked planning is the opportunity to start understanding what are the conceptual steps in the analysis. That way you can keep your hands on the wheel. You can use LLMs to help with planning, but as always, do not take it purely at face value. The context of your experiment is everything and tools can be fickle. It is ultimately up to you to decide what is the ebst appraoch. ## Reproducibility LLMs in general are not reproducible. If I ask the same prompt multiple times I will get different response as the context evolves beyond merely that distinct prompt. Even if someone was able to match the context identically, if someone tries to replicate my work they would also need to use the identical model. Mainstream models like those from Claude and ChatGPT though are dynamic, update, and then retired with limited to access them. If this is the state of play how do you stay reproducible? ## Reproducibility This is the most important step that we are seeing skipped. There are two aspects that are most important to ensure that you stay reproducible. * Always make code * Manage and save your software versions The LLMs should not be covertly running code and making plots without it also saving that code and saving how or where this was ran. ## Always make code You can easily prompt code generation by simply asking for it. Especially when working on my laptop I will have a folder in which I will have data, results and the code which links the two. ## Managing software It doesn't matter if you are running code in R, python, shell scripts etc. What matters is that you have static versions of these software and the packages they use across your analysis. This means once you start on a project you do not update the software. You can use package managers like Conda/Mamba or create containers like Dockers to help manage your software and also enable you to share these with other people or other systems i.e. HPC. You do not need to do this alone though. Setting up these software environments is something that Claude and ChatGPT are pretty good at. Once you are set up you can ensure it takes an appropriate snapshot, then you are good to go. ## What should I do if I can't read the code If you do not understand the code that you are generating take some extra time and break it down. These steps are based on key principles in Bioinformatics that we use when we run new tools or languages we are unfamiliar with. * Ask for annotation of the code - Once annotated read these overviews and ask questions (not just to the LLMs). Add your own additional annotations to help fill in the gaps. * Start small - Only use a small amount of the data. You do not need to run all the data at once. * Tackle the code in steps - When asking for code to run an analysi do not ask for all of it in one go. Instead ask for one step i.e. 1. make code to read in this data 2. add code to normalize the dataset. * Double-check what it is doing - As you work through chunks of code check the saved variables. Do they look as expected? If not, why? * Have known outcomes - Do you have a known positive control? Can you run this code of a dataset that has been previously analyzed and has a known outcome? ## Mananging resources When you are building scripts and planning something that is a little more computationally intensive you should also consider the resources you have available to you. Either on your laptop or on remote servers i.e. HPC systems. Already we suggest running your analysis on a subset to start, so you can make sure the code itself runs ok. Once you have functioning code and are ready to run everything, then you providing information about your computational setup so LLMs can adapt the code to your limits. ## Building Reports We work with reports as the hub for our deliverable analysis. Reports enable us to tie code directly to our output figures in fixed documents. This means no orphan plots where we're not sure exactly how they were generated. Popular examples include Quarto, Rmarkdown and Jupyter. ## Building Reports ## How to check outputs - **Run it.** If code is wrong, it often errors. If it runs, check the output is right. If you don't know what right looks like then you need some positive controls and trial datasets. - **Look it up.** Check arguments against the package help and vignettes. Check anytime it points you to a paper. - **Verify the numbers.** Does it make sense? Export results to spreadsheets so you can manually review. Do directions of changes make sense? Does the normalization make sense? Compare to plots and visualizations. - **Ask for sources, then check them** — As you try to understand what the code is doing and the analysis packages, check the sources. Review the core principles. - **Cross-check.** Ask in a fresh session, or a different model, and compare. Disagreement means look carefully. - **Check the claim, not the style.** If you couldn't have verified it without the model, stop and verify it elsewhere. You remain responsible for everything the tool produces (see *Journal policies* in the LLM Basics section). ## Good practice still applies Good coding practice is still essential when an AI writes the code: - Clear, specific instructions - Working on small subsets of data before the full dataset - Review everything - Planning - Reproducibility - Checkpoints and modularization - Understanding what your code is doing # Hard lines {background-color="#23373B" .center .middle} ## CLAUDE.md and other configuration files ??What CLAUDE.md and similar instruction files are, and how to write them: be specific, set the tone you want?? ## Why rules loosen over time ??Why instructions can weaken over a long session (context compression), and how to guard against it?? ## Controlling what is allowed ??Permission settings, approval prompts, and how to restrict what the AI is allowed to do??
